notes.h: Fire safety when selecting household textiles
notes.b: Household textiles such as curtains, bedding and sofas can feed a fire, so fire risk is a key safety check when buying. How likely a textile is to catch light depends on the structure of the fabric, the fibres in it and the filling inside it.
points: Loosely spun yarns (yarns twisted only lightly, so they trap plenty of air) ignite very easily, so loosely spun fabrics are a poor choice where fire risk is high.
Fabrics with a raised pile or nap (a fluffy surface of upstanding fibres) ignite more easily than smooth, tightly woven fabrics, because flames can run quickly across the loose surface fibres.
Blends of man-made and natural fibres can burn more quickly than either fibre on its own, so a blend is not automatically safer than a single fibre.
Foam and other fillings in cushions and upholstery burn fiercely and give off toxic fumes when they burn, so check what the filling is and whether it is fire resistant.

Flame-retardant treatment lowers the risk of ignition. Inherently flame-retardant fabrics keep their resistance because the fibre itself resists ignition, while coated or finished fabrics rely on a treatment applied to the fabric.

Read the labels for fire-resistance information, for example a statement that the materials meet the requirements for resistance to cigarette and match ignition. Read the care label too, so that a flame-retardant finish is not damaged by washing or cleaning.
Higher-risk items in the home are children's nightwear, upholstered furniture, curtains near heat and protective workwear. Keep textiles away from heaters and cookers.
notes.tip: If asked for two safety considerations when choosing household textiles, pick from loosely spun yarns, a pile surface, fibre blends and the type of filling, and say briefly why each is a risk.

notes.b: A flame-retardant finish is a chemical treatment that reduces how easily a fabric ignites and burns. Proban is one such finish; Pyrovatex is another.
points: Identification: Proban is used on cotton, linen and other cellulosic fabrics (fabrics made from plant cellulose).
Phosphorus and nitrogen compounds are fixed within the fibre structure, so the protection is built into the fibre rather than sitting on the surface as a coating.
You cannot tell by looking or touching whether a fabric has the finish. Its presence is shown on the product label or in the manufacturer's information.
Effect 1: it reduces the flammability of the fabric, which lowers the risk of ignition.

Effect 2: when taken away from a flame the fabric self-extinguishes (goes out by itself), because an insulating char forms around the fibres instead of the fabric burning on. The fabric neither melts nor keeps burning once it is taken away from the flame.
Drawback 1: the finish may cause an allergic reaction in some people.
Drawback 2: the fabric may need special care in cleaning, so follow the care instructions to avoid damaging the finish by washing or cleaning.
Uses: children's nightwear, protective workwear, upholstered furniture, military clothing and curtains, all items where a fire would be particularly dangerous.
notes.tip: Proban makes fabric flame retardant, not fireproof: it reduces burning and the fabric self-extinguishes. Don't confuse a finish applied to a fabric with a fibre that is flame resistant in itself. For two effects, give reduces ignition risk and self-extinguishes; allergy and special cleaning are the drawbacks.

notes.h: Properties of fabric for upholstered furniture
notes.b: Upholstered furniture is sat on every day, so its fabric has to cope with constant use while staying comfortable and safe.
points: Durable and hard wearing: the fabric resists abrasion and rubbing from constant use, so it keeps its appearance and does not wear through or tear.
Resilient: the fabric springs back after being sat on, so cushions keep their shape. Wool is resilient, while cotton loses its shape more readily.
Comfortable: the fabric has a pleasant handle (the feel of the fabric) and is not harsh against the skin.
Stain resistant: spills are less likely to soak in and wipe off more easily. Fabric that is also fade resistant and easy to clean stays looking good for longer.
Fire resistant: the fabric and the filling should resist ignition, and this is shown on a label.

A label stating that the materials meet the requirements for resistance to cigarette and match ignition tells the consumer that the covering has been tested and resists catching fire from a lit cigarette or a match.
notes.tip: For two desirable properties of upholstery fabric, choose from durable, comfortable, resilient, stain resistant and hard wearing. When interpreting a fire-resistance label, say the covering resists ignition from a lit cigarette or a match.

notes.h: Upholstered furniture fire safety requirements (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The rules on the fire safety of domestic upholstered furniture changed in July 2026. The Irish fire safety order for domestic furniture that the syllabus names was revoked (by S.I. 357/2026), and these products now fall under EU product-safety law.
points: From July 2026, the fire safety requirements for domestic upholstered furniture are those of the EU General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR), Regulation (EU) 2023/988.
The GPSR is an EU regulation, so it applies directly in Ireland without needing an Irish Act, and it has applied since 13 December 2024.
Its core duty is that only safe products may be placed on the market. Producers must assess the risks of their products, and sellers, including online sellers, must not supply unsafe goods.

In practice, furniture that meets EU product-safety requirements may be sold to consumers in Ireland. The separate Irish fire label is no longer a legal requirement, though consumers can still look for fire-resistance information from the supplier.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) is the Irish body for consumer information and complaints (ccpc.ie).
notes.tip: If asked what now governs the fire safety of upholstered furniture, name the EU General Product Safety Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/988, and state what it requires: only safe products on the market.

keyTerms.definition: A chemical treatment applied to a textile to reduce its flammability and lower the risk of ignition.
The property of a fabric that stops burning once it is removed from a flame.
The black, insulating carbon layer that forms on a treated fabric when exposed to heat, protecting the fibres beneath.
A surface of loose fibre loops or cut ends on a fabric, which ignites more easily than a smooth surface.
Fire resistance that is built into the fibre itself rather than added by a finish.
The soft covering and padding on furniture, such as the fabric and filling of a sofa or armchair.
The ability of a fabric or filling to spring back to its original shape after being compressed.
Foam in cushions and upholstery burns fiercely and gives off toxic fumes, so check what the filling is and whether it is fire resistant.

factCards.term: Three factors to consider for fire safety in household textiles
factCards.definition: Fabric construction (loose yarns and raised pile ignite easily); the filling material (avoid untreated synthetic foam); and a flame-retardant finish or fire-resistance label.

factCards.term: Two effects of Proban on a fabric
factCards.definition: It reduces the risk of ignition, and it makes the fabric self-extinguish when removed from a flame.
It may cause an allergic reaction, and the treated fabric may need special care during cleaning.

factCards.term: Four textile uses of a flame-retardant finish
factCards.definition: Children's nightwear, protective workwear, upholstered furniture and military clothing.

factCards.term: Meaning of a label stating resistance to cigarette and match ignition
factCards.definition: The materials meet the requirements for resisting ignition from a lit cigarette and from a match.

factCards.term: Legislation for domestic upholstered furniture fire safety from July 2026
factCards.definition: The EU General Product Safety Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/988.

factCards.term: Four desirable properties of fabric for upholstered furniture
factCards.definition: Durable, comfortable, resilient and stain resistant.

questions.prompt: Name one fire-retardant finish used on household textiles and describe one effect it has on a fabric.
questions.model: Proban (or Pyrovatex). Effect: it reduces the flammability of the fabric, lowering the risk of ignition; or it makes the fabric self-extinguish when removed from a flame; or it can cause an allergic reaction in some people, and treated fabric may need special care when cleaned.

questions.prompt: Explain how the choice of fabric, filling and fire-retardant treatment for an upholstered sofa can reduce fire risk in the home.
questions.model: Fabric construction: a smooth, tightly woven fabric is safer than a loosely spun yarn or a fabric with a raised pile, which ignite more easily. Fibre content: a fabric made from one fibre type burns less quickly than a blend of man-made and natural fibres. Filling: untreated synthetic foam releases gases that can ignite and give off toxic fumes, so a combustion-modified high-resilience foam is safer. Treatment: a flame-retardant finish such as Proban reduces ignition risk and makes the fabric self-extinguish when removed from a flame, although the finish may cause an allergic reaction or need careful cleaning. Labelling: a label showing resistance to cigarette and match ignition confirms the fabric and filling have been tested. From July 2026, the fire safety requirements for domestic upholstered furniture are those of the EU General Product Safety Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/988.
